you-are-a-business-of-one.core: Treat your career like a business: your skills are the product, employers are clients, and compensation is the contract. Companies negotiate professionally every day; negotiating your offer is expected, rarely risks the offer, and compounds over a career through raises and future offers.

first_principles.problem: An engineer accepts the first offer and leaves tens of thousands per year on the table, compounding for years.
truths: Future raises are percentages of the base.

analogy.title: A consultant pricing a contract
analogy.story: They quote based on value and market, not on what they'd grudgingly accept.
analogy.breaks: Consultants juggle many clients; you usually have one employer at a time, which makes alternatives vital.

example.title: Compounding a $10k difference
flow: 3% annual raises on a higher base
Next jobs anchor on current pay
example.outcome: negotiation seen as a professional duty.

check.q: Why does negotiating base salary compound?
check.a: Raises, bonuses and future offers are often calculated from or anchored on your current base.

the-batna-your-source-of-confidence.core: BATNA is your Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement: what you'll do if this deal fails (another offer, staying put, a retention package). A strong BATNA gives real leverage and calm confidence; improving it, by interviewing in parallel, is the most powerful negotiation move.

first_principles.problem: With no other options, a candidate feels they must accept anything.
derivation: **Interview in parallel** and time offers together.
**Value** your current job honestly as a BATNA.

analogy.title: Buying a car when you have another dealer's quote
analogy.story: You can calmly walk away, and the salesperson knows it.
analogy.breaks: Car prices are fairly transparent; comp bands are often hidden, so data matters more.

example.title: Aligning offer timing
flow: Ask for a week to decide

check.q: What's the best way to strengthen your BATNA?
check.a: Run multiple interview processes in parallel so offers arrive close together.

anchoring-who-names-a-number-first.core: The first number mentioned anchors the negotiation, so subsequent offers adjust around it. Avoid naming a low number early ('I'm focusing on fit; I'll consider a competitive offer'); if you must give one, anchor high with a researched range whose bottom you'd be happy with, framed around market data.

first_principles.problem: Asked for expectations on the first call, a candidate names a modest number and the offer lands exactly there.
truths: Companies have bands you don't see.
derivation: If pressed, give a **researched, high range**.
Never disclose **current salary** where avoidable or illegal to ask.

analogy.title: Bidding at a market stall
analogy.story: Whoever names the first price sets the starting point for haggling.
analogy.breaks: Market stalls expect theatrics; corporate negotiation rewards calm, data-backed framing.

example.title: Recruiter screen script
flow: 'I'm focused on finding the right role; I'm confident we'll find a number that works. What's the band for this level?'

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: You learn their range without capping yourself.

check.q: Why avoid naming a number first?
check.a: It anchors the negotiation and may be below the company's budget, capping your offer.

public-equity-rsus-treat-it-like-cash.core: RSUs at public companies are shares that vest over time (often 4 years, sometimes front- or back-loaded). Because they're liquid on vest, treat them like cash compensation that fluctuates with the stock price, and evaluate offers on annual total comp: base + bonus + RSU value per year.

first_principles.problem: A candidate compares offers by base salary and misses $80k/year of RSU difference.
truths: Vested public shares can be sold immediately.
derivation: Compute **annual RSU value** = grant ÷ vesting years (per the schedule).

analogy.title: A salary partly paid in a foreign currency
analogy.story: It's real money, but the exchange rate changes.
analogy.breaks: Currencies rarely drop 50% in a year; tech stocks sometimes do.

example.title: Comparing two offers
flow: A is $50k/yr more despite lower base

steps.label: Check
steps.detail: Look at vesting schedules and refreshers too.

check.q: Why consider selling RSUs on vest?
check.a: Holding concentrates your wealth and job in one company's stock; selling is like receiving cash bonus and choosing to buy stock.

pre-ipo-equity-lottery-tickets-with-math.core: Startup equity (options or RSUs) is illiquid and uncertain: value depends on exit, dilution, preferences and strike price. Model it with scenarios (failure, modest exit, big exit) and probabilities, understand option exercise costs and windows, and value it far below the paper price.

first_principles.problem: A candidate takes a 30% pay cut for options that become worthless after liquidation preferences.
truths: Most startups don't produce large exits.
Options cost money to exercise and may be taxed.
derivation: Ask: **% ownership**, fully diluted shares, latest **preferred price**, **409A**, **strike**.
Know **exercise window** after leaving (90 days vs 10 years).

analogy.title: A lottery ticket where you can calculate the odds
analogy.story: It might pay off hugely, but you shouldn't count it as rent money.
analogy.breaks: Lottery odds are fixed; your work can slightly improve the startup's odds.

example.title: Expected value of options

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Weigh EV against the high chance of nothing.

example.outcome: a realistic view of startup equity.

check.q: Why does ownership percentage matter more than number of options?
check.a: Share counts are meaningless without the total fully diluted shares; percentage tells you your slice of an exit.

equity-refreshers-the-golden-handcuffs.core: Refreshers are additional equity grants given yearly or for performance, which keep total comp from collapsing after the initial grant vests (the 'year-5 cliff'). Overlapping vesting schedules create golden handcuffs: leaving forfeits unvested shares, so new offers must compensate.

first_principles.problem: An engineer's comp drops 40% in year five because the initial grant finished vesting and refreshers were small.
truths: Initial grants are front-weighted in value.
Unvested equity is what you give up when leaving.
derivation: Ask about **refresher policy** and typical sizes.
Ask new employers for a **sign-on/make-whole** grant.

analogy.title: A layered subscription that keeps renewing
analogy.story: Each year adds a new layer that pays out over the next few years.
analogy.breaks: Subscriptions charge you; here the layers pay you, which is why they bind you.

steps.label: Negotiation
steps.detail: New offer adds $120k sign-on to cover forfeited shares.

check.a: Extra equity or cash from a new employer to compensate for unvested equity you forfeit by leaving.

the-negotiation-conversation-scripts-and.core: Effective negotiation is collaborative and specific: express enthusiasm, state a concrete ask backed by data or competing offers, focus on the components with flexibility (sign-on, equity, level), use silence, get everything in writing, and never accept on the spot.

first_principles.problem: A candidate says 'Can you do any better?', gets $2k more, and feels awkward pushing further.

analogy.title: Two people planning a trip together
analogy.story: Both want it to happen; you're working out the details, not fighting.
analogy.breaks: Trip partners share costs equally; employers have budgets and approval chains you can't see.

example.title: A counteroffer script
flow: 'I'm really excited about the team and the role.'
'I have an offer at $320k total; I'd love to make this work.'
'If you can get to $340k, ideally via equity, I'm ready to sign.'

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Recruiter returns with +$25k RSU and $15k sign-on.

example.outcome: a better offer with goodwill intact.

check.q: Why say 'If you can get to X, I'll sign'?
check.a: It gives the recruiter a concrete, closable target to justify internally.
